events.excerpt: I never think much about buoys unless I’m watching a movie about man-eating sharks. But it turns out they don’t just float out on there on the ocean for the nice aesthetics; they’re there for a reason. Wave buoys, for instance, are there primarily to measure wave activity. And like everything else these days, the information they provide is available online. TheMaritimePilot used that data to build this desktop model that mirrors the movement of a selected real-life buoy . TheMaritimePilot happens to be a maritime pilot in Belgium, so his work relies on the data provided by wave buoys. So, this idea makes perfect sense for him. But I think everyone else will appreciate it, too. This is called SeaGlance and it is a small buoy, a few inches tall, that bounces around on virtual waves rolling across a desk. Of course, there aren’t any actual waves and so the buoy actually rides from a series of cables. Eight stepper motors can pool those cables in and out, moving the buoy up and down — and even tilting it side-to-side. SeaGlance turns those motors according to live data that it fetches over Wi-Fi. SeaGlance can grab data from a variety of different sources. Many of them are country-specific and provided by those country’s relevant agencies, but they’re usually freely available to eve
events.headline: This Actuated Desktop Model Mirrors the Movement of a Real-Life Buoy

events.excerpt: A microphone is an odd — and somewhat disturbing — thing to find inside a coffee machine. That's what caught the attention of hardware hacker Robin M., who spotted one mentioned in the service documentation for a Spengler PSL50. What started as an attempt to figure out why it was there quickly turned into a much bigger hardware hacking project involving embedded Linux, an unsecured debug interface, a questionable USB update system, and, of course, Doom . According to the machine's supplier, the microphone was intended for future presence detection and accessibility features, but wasn't actually being used. Further investigation was unwelcome, so Robin took another route: buying a spare display/controller module on eBay and poking around inside it. The board turned out to be pretty complex for a coffee machine. It was built around an NXP i.MX 6 processor with an Arm Cortex-A9 core, running a Yocto-based embedded Linux system. The hardware also includes Ethernet, USB, microSD storage, and interfaces for payment hardware, cup dispensers, energy-saving modules, and more. After tracing the power circuitry and supplying the board with 24 volts, Robin got it running on the bench. events.excerpt: TL;DR A contract on Base checks every Zcash block header against Zcash’s consensus rules: the Equihash (200, 9) solution on the EIP-152 BLAKE2b precompile, the difficulty adjustment (including NU7’s 25-second blocks), the time rules and cumulative work. Contracts can then read Zcash’s best chain without trusting a bridge, a committee or whoever relays. Anyone can feed it; a feeder can delay the relay but cannot make it accept a header Zcash’s rules reject. One header costs about 626k gas (mean, whole transaction); Equihash is 361k of it. Following Zcash at 25-second blocks is ~3,456 headers, ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ gas a day: about 0.01 ETH a day at Base’s 0.005 gwei. A relay deployed with Mainnet parameters on 29 October 2026 crossed Zcash Mainnet’s NU7 activation (height 3,543,405, 6 November 2026) without a redeploy and followed the 5,405 headers after it. On top of the relay: a RISC Zero proof (Groth16-wrapped, 256,720 gas to verify on Base) that a shielded payment of at least an amount went to a receiver an app committed to, with a memo naming the app’s reference, inside the ZIP 221 chain history of a header the relay holds. The transaction id, the note, the block and the address never reach the EVM chain. A real Testnet payment was proven in 81 s on a rented RTX 4090, for about one cen
events.headline: Seam: verifying Zcash headers on Base with EIP-152, and proving shielded payments without linking the chains

events.excerpt: This release brings various stability improvements, ECDSA TX-form binding, and improved replica 2.9 syncing. We recommend installing it as soon as you can to address potential node stability issues. Configuration Note: the first time you start the node after upgrading to N.2.9.8, do not use the start_from_local_state or start_from_block configuration options. Syncing: Syncing could slow down to the pace of the slowest peer, even when much faster peers were available. Each storage module limits how much sync work it keeps in progress at once. When the node reached data that only a slow peer had, that peer's requests could take up the whole limit, and the node stopped moving on to the rest of the data. The faster peers that had the rest sat idle until the slow peer was done, which could take days. Restarts made this more likely. The node kept its sync position in memory only, so after a restart every storage module started over from the beginning. If the first missing data there was only available from slow peers, the storage module synced at their pace. We reproduced both cases in the sync simulator and fixed them: A single peer can now take up at most half of a storage module's sync work limit. events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it del
events.headline: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore
events.headline: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

While hobbyists can buy LCD and OLED panels in many shapes and sizes, creating a custom display that fits an unusual surface or application requires specialized equipment and a lot of expertise. Researchers at the University of Bath have developed a new technique that could change that, making it possible to fabricate high-resolution electroluminescent displays using little more than an airbrush and a laser cutter. The technique, called Spray and Etch , combines the simplicity of spraying conductive and electroluminescent materials onto a surface with the precision of laser etching to create detailed patterns and individually addressable pixels. Unlike conventional display fabrication methods, it doesn't require expensive industrial equipment or complicated masking procedures. The process begins by spraying a thin layer of conductive copper-based ink onto a substrate. A standard, unmodified CO2 laser cutter then removes selected portions of the coating to form precisely defined electrodes. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. events.excerpt: Bitcoin Core has published a high-severity advisory disclosing a bug that could prevent affected nodes from creating block templates after a blockchain reorganization. While the flaw didn’t change Bitcoin’s consensus rules, it could leave a miner unable to produce blocks until the node was restarted. How a Reorg Can Leave the Mempool Broken The advisory, CVE-2025-62861, is about an inconsistency involving version 3 transactions, known as TRUC, and Bitcoin Core’s mempool, with the affected releases being versions 28.0 to 28.2 and 29.0 to 29.1. Under BIP-431, TRUC transactions face extra mempool restrictions where each can only have one unconfirmed ancestor (earlier transactions) and one unconfirmed descendant (later transactions). It should be noted that these are relay policy rules and not consensus requirements, meaning valid blocks can have arrangements that the mempool rejects. “When a transaction submitted to the mempool would give a TRUC parent a second unconfirmed child, Bitcoin Core’s ‘sibling eviction’ logic (introduced in v28.0) treats the existing child as a replacement candidate and, if the new transaction pays enough, evicts it under replace-by-fee rules,” read the advisory. According to the Bitcoin Core team, the above flaw usually appears during a chain reorganizati
events.headline: This Is Why Some Bitcoin Core Nodes Can Stop Building Blocks

These properties make it particularly attractive for applications that require short bursts of enormous electrical power, such as pulsed lasers, medical imaging equipment, and nuclear fusion systems. events.excerpt: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show
events.headline: OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
